ANIMATION RIGS

Eight stick-figure rigs live in a grey-box course: two flights of stairs over a platform, and a ladder up a tower with a big red button on top.

CAMERA

Drag to orbit. Pinch or scroll to zoom. Two fingers (or right-drag / shift-drag) to pan. Tap a figure to follow it, tap empty space to let go. Tap the button yourself if you like. The speed menu top-right runs time at 4×, 2×, 1×, ½× or ¼× so you can study the gait; the version menu beside it switches the animation model live, so the same figures can be compared under each.

VERSIONS

A002 (default) adds the body-mass model, balance, smoothing and torso sway described below. A001 is the first release, kept exactly as it shipped. Add ?v=A001 to the address to open on an older version.

THE RIG

Every figure is 21 joints: pelvis, two spine joints, neck and head, then shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand per arm and hip, knee, ankle and toe per leg. Bone lengths never change. Legs and arms are solved every frame with two-bone inverse kinematics: the code decides where a foot or hand should be, and the knee or elbow is placed analytically, bent toward a pole direction (knees forward, elbows back and out).

WALKING AND RUNNING

Feet are planted in the world and only move during their swing, so they never skate. When a foot lifts, its landing spot is predicted from the body's velocity so it lands under the hips at mid-stance. On stairs the landing is snapped to the centre of a tread: one tread per step walking, two running. The heel peels up late in each stance, the toe pitches through the swing, the pelvis bobs (lowest at mid-stance when running, highest when walking) and is pulled down whenever a leg could not reach, and the arms and shoulders counter-swing the legs. Turning on the spot re-plants the feet.

BALANCE (A002)

Each figure has a body-mass model: fourteen segments (head and neck 8.1% of body mass, trunk 49.7%, each upper arm 2.8%, forearm 1.6%, hand 0.6%, thigh 10%, shank 4.65%, foot 1.45%) with each segment's own centre of mass placed along it from published anthropometric tables (source: Winter, Biomechanics and Motor Control of Human Movement, after Dempster 1955). Every frame the whole-body centre of mass is computed from the actual pose and moved to where the support says it must be. Walking, that is solved with trunk lean: on stairs the upper foot carries the body, so climbing leans the trunk forward over the step ahead; speeding up needs the centre of mass ahead of the feet (acceleration × height ÷ g), slowing down behind them. Reaching for the button keeps the trunk where the reach puts it and slides the hips back instead, as people do. Getting up off the floor leans as far forward as it must to bring the mass over the feet before rising.

Side to side, the mass shifts toward whichever foot is carrying weight: part-way when walking, almost fully when standing. The hip of the swinging leg drops about 4° and the trunk leans slightly toward the stance side. The pelvis rises and falls twice per stride. Standing, figures breathe, sway a centimetre or so, and every few seconds settle their weight onto one leg.

Smoothing: each foot's swing runs on its own clock and starts from where the heel actually lifted, rising and landing with zero vertical speed; the landing spot glides toward the prediction and is committed before touch-down; on stairs each step lands one tread beyond the other foot, and the foot clears each riser by following the stair profile rather than a timing curve; the heel strikes first and the foot rolls flat. Knees and elbows bend in the limb's own plane and ease toward straight instead of snapping straight. Pelvis height, lean, sway and head pitch move on critically damped springs, so no target change ever jolts them; pose changes blend from where each joint was heading, not from a frozen snapshot. Ladder hand-offs blend instead of switching, and figures are never shoved apart faster than they can walk.

THE LADDER

Climbing moves the limbs in diagonal pairs, left hand with right foot and then the other pair, each up two rungs at a time, while the pelvis rises steadily. Getting on, mounting the platform and stepping off are their own keyed transitions, again with IK limbs.

THE BUTTON

Whoever reaches the top walks to the button and presses it. The treads fold into a slide, everyone standing on either flight loses their footing, falls onto their back, turns feet-first and slides down under gravity and friction, then gets up. The slides turn back into stairs a few seconds later, and never while anyone is still on them. A press while the slides are out does nothing; the button only glows when it is armed.

THE QUEUE

One ladder, one climber at a time. Whenever someone is on the ladder or the tower, another figure walks over and waits at the foot of the ladder to go up next; someone waiting at the top to come down goes first.

RENDERING

No 3D library: a hand-written perspective projection onto a 2D canvas. Surfaces are split into small tiles, back faces are culled, everything is drawn far-to-near, and walls are flat-shaded from one sun direction whose shadows are projected onto the floor.
